Drawing on Resource Orchestration Theory and Institutional Theory, the study identifies three causal mechanisms through which reshoring facilitates circular economy practices: internal production control as an enabler of integration and experimentation; supply base reconfiguration towards innovative local SMEs as an enabler of co-development of circular components; and the creation of a local innovation ecosystem as an enabler of systemic value change. The activation of these mechanisms is contingent on institutional and contextual conditions, such as regulatory incentives and supply chain realities, suggesting that reshoring alone is insufficient to drive circularity.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2684340.a: Grounded in middle-range theory (MRT), this study explores supply chain resilience (SCRes) during the 2021 Henan floods through 54 interviews with agri-food industry practitioners. The findings reveal SCRes to be a multi-level framework determined by individuals, organizations, supply chains, and broader environments collectively. The environmental level, comprising political, economic, social, technological, environmental, legal, and cultural (PESTELC) factors, functions as the resource layer, providing critical resources. The supply chain level is the direction layer, setting goals for preparation, response, recovery, and adaptation by the organizations and individuals involved. The organizational level is the transmission layer, disseminating resilience objectives both horizontally and vertically. Finally, the individual level is the implementation layer, operationalizing organizational and SCRes strategies. Organizational employees’ personal attributes, such as openness, persistence, and extraversion, should be carefully considered when implementing SCRes strategies. China’s hierarchical culture, chain leader system, and accountability mechanisms ensure coordination across all levels.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2685256.a: Grounded in social exchange and social network theories, we study whether and how buyer firms’ social sustainability draws on their suppliers’ digital technology-oriented open innovation (DTOI). We focus on two dimensions of buyer social sustainability, namely societal and workforce sustainability, and examine the moderating role of buyers’ director network structure. Using panel data on Chinese listed firms from 2014 to 2024, we find that both dimensions are positively associated with supplier DTOI. These relationships are stronger for buyers whose director networks feature higher degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and structural holes, but not closeness centrality. We further explore how these relationships vary across relational, ownership, and industry contexts. Our findings extend digital innovation research to supply chains and clarify when supplier spillovers reach buyers.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2687599.a: This paper operationalizes the Fifth Hand, an emergent theory of project behavior explaining cost misperformance in infrastructure projects, through a neo-institutional response matrix that captures institutional pressure and behavioral enactment across two governance regimes: (1) the pre-contract regime, where funding commitments are established at the decision-to-build; and (2) the post-contract regime, where delivery proceeds under contractual enforcement and audit oversight. Two indices—the Mode of Action Index and the Institutional Pressure Index—classify cost-relevant decision episodes and identify patterns of dominance, transition, entrenchment, and suppression across regimes. An illustrative case, the New Perth Bunbury Highway, shows how cost trajectories emerge from governance responses to divergence between approved funding and updated cost projections. Under heightened institutional pressure, adjustments are deferred, increasing the likelihood of discrete increases in funding. Under moderated pressure, revised projections are incorporated earlier through incremental adjustment. The response matrix explains how cost misperformance develops through successive governance decisions.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2687600.a: The fashion and textile industry comprises complex supply chain operations with significant environmental impacts, highlighting the importance of integrating sustainable manufacturing practices. This exploratory case study investigates the implementation of environmental sustainability practices in upstream fashion manufacturing, focusing on how operations adopt, manage, and operationalise these practices. An inductive approach was adopted, drawing on semi-structured interviews with 43 manufacturing practitioners, followed by within-case and cross-case analysis. The findings provide comprehensive insight into the diversity and complexity of environmental issues, identifying 25 indicators of sustainable practices, 23 indicators of unsustainable practices and the multifaceted nature of their implementation. The study categorises a wide range of sustainable practices, identifies critical areas requiring improvement, and outlines practical strategies supported by a process map to guide operational adoption. A conceptual model is developed to advance theoretical insights and practical implementation of environmental sustainability in fashion manufacturing. Although based in the fashion industry, the findings provide transferable insights applicable to multi-tier supply chains across manufacturing sectors, benefiting wider stakeholders and sustainability transitions.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2687605.a: Despite increasing managerial interest, many firms struggle to scale sustainable servitization initiatives beyond pilot projects, facing capability misalignments, measurement challenges and governance complexities. This paper proposes a maturity model to assess and support manufacturing firms’ transition towards sustainable servitization. We structure and populate the model through a systematic literature review complemented by 19 interviews with managers, consultants and academics, and we subsequently test and deploy it in four companies. Our analysis shows that sustainable servitization is enabled by 11 capabilities, which we articulate into 62 items. These items populate 7 maturity dimensions and can be evaluated on five-level scales. The resulting model consolidates the fragmented sustainable servitization literature by identifying the capabilities that enable this transformation. In practice, it can be used to identify structured maturity profiles, support both internal analysis and cross-company benchmarking, guide targeted capability-development roadmaps and raise awareness of sustainable servitization opportunities, even in low-maturity contexts.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2687606.a: While product platforms in vertically-integrated firms are well studied, prior explanations become limited where platforming firms face tensions between openness and control in managing supply-chains. This paper explores how construction firms govern supply-chain interactions through digitally-enabled product platforms with varying interface openness. Drawing on a comparative case study of four firms, the research establishes that process embedding and process generativity serve as common foundational mechanisms required to bridge physical production constraints and digital workflows. Furthermore, the study provides new insight on process streamlining and process improvement as the distinctive control mechanisms used to dynamically adjust supply-chain governance. Depending on interface openness, firms configure proprietary or democratised process streamlining to control data flows and stakeholder workflows. Simultaneously, they deploy highly centralised or self-initiating process improvement loops to maintain authority over platform evolution. The paper extends platform governance theory from a physical-digital setting, by providing strategies to resolve the openness paradox and retain control over value creation.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2691568.a: The rapid diffusion of emerging technologies is redefining how operations are designed and managed, shifting attention from techno-centric efficiency to socio-technical integration. This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, 3D printing, blockchain, immersive environments, and IoT-5G reshape operational processes and human–machine interactions. Drawing on Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory and an Empirically Grounded Analytics approach, 10,559 operational practices were analysed through co-occurrence and correlation mapping. By comparing six technologies across eight socio-technical dimensions, results indicate that AI and robotics strongly relate to augmentation and data-driven decision-making, blockchain and IoT-5G enhance safety, traceability, and distributed control, and immersive environments foster engagement and experiential learning. These findings show that emerging technologies reshape operational architectures by redistributing decision authority, altering coordination mechanisms, and transforming the role of human participation. Moreover, thirteen empirically grounded propositions extend STS theory, offering a socio-technical framework for managing digital transformation in operations management.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2695691.a: The transition towards low-carbon and digitally enabled manufacturing requires an integrated understanding of Quality Management (QM), Industry 4.0 (I4.0) and Industrial Decarbonization (ID) capabilities. However, existing maturity models (MMs) assess these domains in isolation. This study develops and applies a capability-based MM that evaluates the integrated maturity of QM–I4.0–ID in manufacturing organizations. Grounded in Design Science Research, the MM expands a framework comprising 49 organizational capabilities and 11 dimensions. Those are algorithmically linked within the model’s back end. The MM was validated and preliminarily applied in 17 manufacturing firms. Findings from an automotive manufacturer demonstrate heterogeneous maturity profiles, as decarbonization performance coexists with limited digital or managerial integration. The dashboards and multi-level diagnostics provide actionable insights for strategic decision-making. The study contributes to theory with an integrated perspective on digitalization and sustainability. Further, it offers practitioners and policymakers a prescriptive tool to guide structured maturity improvement pathways.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2695694.a: Despite growing interest in digital technologies for socially sustainable supply chain management, their contribution to social sustainability remains constrained by governance-relevant information failures. This conceptual development paper theorises satellite-enabled evidentiary governance: a bounded process through which satellite technologies and artificial intelligence may strengthen socially sustainable supply chain governance by altering the evidentiary basis for surfacing, prioritising, verifying, and accounting for weakly observable risks. Building on a socio-technical governance perspective, institutional theory, and contingency logic, I argue that satellites create value not by delivering universal transparency or directly revealing social harm, but by providing an independent, repeated, large-scale, and place-based observational layer that complements audits, supplier disclosures, traceability systems, and other digital tools. The framework identifies four governance translation mechanisms: risk surfacing, prioritisation, targeted verification, and evidentiary accountability. It also specifies boundary conditions. The paper contributes by shifting attention from visibility as disclosure to evidentiary governance in socially sustainable supply chains.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2695697.a: Safety is a critical yet neglected dimension of sustainability in battery closed-loop supply chains. Circular economy practices within it introduce safety challenges that require coordination across stakeholders,making blockchain a promising enabler. However, effective blockchain implementation is hindered by unclear stakeholder roles.Drawing on stakeholder and resource dependence theories, this study applies the responsible, accountable, consulted, informed matrix with power and involvement dimensions to define stakeholder roles.Results show that upstream actors, investors and technology providers occupy responsible role; governments are accountable and downstream actors are informed. No stakeholder occupies the consulted role, reflecting the dominance of operational responsibility over advisory coordination at this early stage of blockchain integration. Perceptual differences further reveal ambiguity in stakeholder roles. These findings extend stakeholder theory by grounding salience in measurable resource-dependence dimensions, advance resource dependence theory by demonstrating its temporal dynamics across technology lifecycles, and offer practitioners a methodology for blockchain integration in supply chains.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2696989.a: The success of implementing circular economy practices at the micro level depends on the assessment frameworks used to monitor progress and identify opportunities for improvement. In this regard, maturity models play a crucial role, as they encourage companies to evolve to a higher maturity level. However, as maturity is a practice-based concept, its evaluation relies on human judgement, which is often imprecise and vague. Focusing on this aspect, this article introduces a novel fuzzy-based maturity model for assessing circular economy practices in manufacturing firms. The model generates an overall maturity index to classify firms into five distinct maturity stages and guide the identification of improvement priorities. The assessment approach was empirically tested across three manufacturing plants, confirming its applicability and practical contribution. From a theoretical perspective, the model contributes to the field by incorporating the subjectivity inherent in circular maturity assessments. For practitioners, the model serves as a self-assessment tool to prioritise circular practices.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2703532.a: Reference class forecasting (RCF) has become a central tool in infrastructure investment governance, primarily supporting funding approval by comparing outcomes with those of completed projects. Cost overruns that arise between funding commitment and contract award, and subsequently during construction, are often tied to how risk and uncertainty are managed after project approval, particularly when RCF is used to set or control contingency allowances. These patterns point to a problem in post-approval uncertainty management rather than a limitation of cost-estimation methods alone. While RCF provides a useful assurance mechanism for testing the plausibility of proposed cost estimates, it is not designed to manage uncertainty during the pre-contract phase, when project-specific information remains incomplete and subject to revision. A decomposed contingency approach (DCA) is proposed as a conceptual and methodological framework for managing uncertainty during this period. The DCA distinguishes among risk and aleatory uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty arising from incomplete or provisional information, and residual uncertainty associated with system-level effects that cannot be fully anticipated. It links different forms of uncertainty to decision approaches suited to their informational characteristics and provides a structured basis for adjusting contingency as information becomes more complete. Within this framework, contingency is determined through a decomposed treatment of uncertainty, while RCF is retained solely as an independent assurance mechanism.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2703533.a: Manufacturing firms seeking to implement circular economy strategies often face a practical challenge in translating R-imperatives into coordinated decisions on product development and supply chain design. Although prior studies and conceptual frameworks have highlighted the importance of integrating these domains, there is limited guidance on how to operationalise such integration in practice. In response, this study develops a three-phase operationalisation framework for integrating R-imperatives, product development, and supply chain design. The framework comprises an As-Is phase, which identifies the current product and supply chain configuration and assesses the existing level of integration, a To-Be phase, which identifies feasible R-imperatives and the redesign requirements they imply, and a To-Do phase, which identifies implementation challenges, capability gaps, and action priorities. The framework is built on the existing knowledge in the literature and empirically grounded through multiple case studies of Norwegian manufacturing companies. The findings show that the feasibility of R-imperatives depends strongly on product architecture, reverse logistics capabilities, and the synchronisation between product redesign and supply chain adaptation. The study contributes by moving beyond conceptual recognition of integration towards a practical framework that supports design for circularity in industrial settings.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2703538.a: Sustainable supplier selection in the textile and apparel industry is hindered by generic criteria and the difficulty of balancing expert cognitive efficiency with ranking robustness. This study develops a textile-specific indicator system with 23 indicators, screened from 42 candidates via the Content Validity Ratio (CVR) by 13 industry experts, and proposes an integrated fuzzy MCDM framework combining Fuzzy Best-Worst Method (Fuzzy-BWM) and Triangular Fuzzy Number-MULTIMOORA (TFN-MULTIMOORA). In a case study of a Chinese apparel trading enterprise and six core suppliers, the economic dimension received the highest weight (0.453), followed by the social (0.279) and environmental (0.267) dimensions, while product quality (0.068) and strategic decision-making and execution ability (0.058) were the most influential sub-indicators. Supplier S3 ranked first across the Ratio System, Reference Point and Full Multiplicative Form. Cross-method validation with four alternative fuzzy MCDM methods yielded a mean Spearman rank correlation of 0.903, and sensitivity analysis under 16 weight variation scenarios produced a mean Spearman correlation of 0.966. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides a textile-specific, cognitively efficient and robust alternative to existing sustainable supplier selection approaches.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2704642.a: Construction constraints are a foundational concept in Lean Construction. They are factors that restrict or regulate the execution of tasks and hinder workflow reliability. Their systematic identification and removal underpin production planning and control processes such as the Last Planner System (LPS). However, current constraint management (CM) has yet to reach sufficient implementation levels in most projects. Motivated by the need to improve CM in current construction practices, this article aims to identify current research gaps through a state-of-the-art review of CM-related research and propose future directions for addressing the gaps. To achieve this, we conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) using a sequential mixed-method design, combining bibliometric analysis (quantitative mapping) with thematic analysis (qualitative synthesis). First, a total of 128 papers were collected using a structured data collection approach from Scopus and the IGLC (International Group for Lean Construction) conference and then fed into a bibliometric analysis to construct science maps. Subsequently, an in-depth thematic analysis combined with the quantitative analysis results is presented to reveal the research topics, trends, gaps, and future directions of CM-related research. As a consequence, five primary research themes, along with their research trends and gaps, have been revealed. This article suggests five areas for improvement to overcome the identified gaps in current CM-related research. Through its findings and recommendations, this article contributes to the body of knowledge of CM-related research and provides future directions to enhance CM implementation in construction projects.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2705968.a: This study examines the relationship between the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in production processes and product innovation outcomes in manufacturing firms. It contributes to the literature by providing empirical evidence on the role of AI in innovation while accounting for firm-level heterogeneity in established innovation drivers, including R&D intensity, workforce qualifications, human-centric practices, and structural characteristics. Using data from 1,334 firms in the 2022 German Manufacturing Survey, we find that AI implementation in production is positively associated with innovation-enhancing processes that complement existing organisational resources and capabilities. However, this relationship is limited to product innovations that are new to the firm and does not extend to innovations that are new to the market. Furthermore, distinguishing between product innovation types relevant to the twin transition, we find that AI implementation is primarily associated with a higher likelihood of digital product innovations, whereas eco-oriented product innovations are more strongly linked to the adoption of human-centric practices. These findings suggest that AI in production should be viewed not merely as an operational technology but as a strategic capability whose innovation potential depends on its integration with complementary organisational resources and capabilities.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2705970.a: Drawing on a lean inventory perspective, this study examines how digitalisation empowers inventory management. Using panel data on firms listed on China’s A-share market, we find that firm digitalisation significantly increases inventory leanness, which in turn enhances firm value. Mechanism analyses show that digitalisation improves inventory management efficiency primarily through an internal optimisation channel (increasing production efficiency), and an external integration channel (enhancing supply chain efficiency). In addition, digitalisation improves inventory management efficiency by reducing sales uncertainty. This study provides empirical evidence on the mechanisms through which digitalisation empowers inventory management and enables firms to optimise inventory management and enhance firm value through digital transformation.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2705976.a: Recent literature increasingly emphasizes the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies into supply chain (SC) management. Among these, Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence (AI) have attracted growing academic and managerial interest, although research remains at an early stage. This study maps the evolution, intellectual structure, and emerging themes of Blockchain and AI research in SCs. It analyzes all relevant Scopus-indexed articles published from the earliest available record through 2024. Bibliometric analysis and science mapping are conducted using VOSviewer and SciMAT. Findings indicate that research was limited and fragmented until early 2022, followed by rapid growth and thematic consolidation between 2022 and 2024. The study contributes by jointly reviewing Blockchain and AI literature in SCs, identifying major thematic clusters, comparing their separate and combined applications, and deriving managerial, operational, and future research implications. It also provides a forward-looking reference for developing planning and control strategies in Blockchain-AI-enabled SCs and practical implementation efforts.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2708088.a: With the trend of globalisation, manufacturing companies configure their supply networks and transfer production facilities from one location to another. Whilst current literature mainly focuses on factors affecting production relocations, less is known about the implementation process which contains evolving activities across manufacturing and supply levels. In this paper, we ask the following research question: How do firms implement their production relocation process, when considering the impacts of manufacturing and supply networks? Through a longitudinal case study of a manufacturing company in Taiwan, we develop a process-oriented framework with five phases, namely preparation, manufacturing network relocation, supply network relocation, network development, and network integration. Our study further highlights the interdependent connection between manufacturing networks and supply networks. The study provides guidance to companies which are involved in production relocation decisions in the changing international business context.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2709637.a: This his study examines how digital maturity models can more effectively guide Industry 4.0 implementation in manufacturing contexts. Despite the proliferation of maturity and readiness models, firms still struggle to translate assessments into actionable improvements aligned with operational objectives. Existing models tend to emphasize specific technologies or isolated dimensions, limiting their ability to capture the systemic nature of digital transformation and the learning processes embedded in its implementation. This study adopts a Design Science Research approach to develop a maturity assessment framework grounded in operational targets. The model departs from technology-centric perspectives and structures digital maturity around recurring manufacturing challenges across four dimensions: Smart Manufacturing, Smart Supply Chain, Smart Working and Smart Consumption. The framework was co-developed and validated through an iterative, longitudinal process with a large manufacturing company, integrating literature analysis, field observations, interviews, benchmarking and real-world applications. The resulting model defines sixteen operational targets across six maturity levels, enabling firms to link technology adoption to measurable operational improvements. The findings also emphasize the role of the development and implementation process as a source of organizational learning.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2711340.a: The adoption of smart sustainable practices is important for improving construction performance and resilience; however, their implementation in Malaysia remains constrained by barriers. This study develops a multilevel understanding of these barriers and their potential implications for project delivery performance. A survey of 101 construction professionals was analysed using descriptive statistics and exploratory factor analysis. Twenty barriers were identified, with the most critical being the lack of financial resources, the lack of standards and policies, resistance to change, lack of awareness and low market demand. Six latent dimensions emerged: organizational readiness and industry acceptance; technical capability and organizational integration barriers; institutional support deficiency; perceived risk and workforce adaptation barriers; project coordination and system integration barriers; and strategic leadership deficiency. Guided primarily by the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, the findings were synthesized into the Smart Sustainable Construction Barriers Model (SSC-BM), linking barriers to organizational, technological and institutional constraints. The model conceptually links upstream weaknesses to downstream inefficiencies in workflow coordination, planning reliability and production control. Overall, the study provides a framework for improving smart sustainable construction adoption through a theory-informed interpretation of its implications for project delivery performance rather than empirical validation of causal relationships.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2711341.a: Digital twins lack a common understanding in the literature, and their impact on operations and supply chain management should be further explored to realise the technology’s potential value. Conducting a multi-round Delphi survey with additional expert interviews, we identify the underlying technical components, functionalities, and adoption barriers. Subsequently, we derive a detailed framework that provides an overview of the digital twin characteristics at the product, process, or system level. We examine multiple impact areas of digital twins related to operational excellence, risk management, communication, and innovation. Our Delphi ranking shows that digital twins could affect production process reliability, setup, and testing of machinery and maintenance procedures. We also employ the CIMO logic to inform our discussion of the potential underlying mechanisms. Our study works towards a shared holistic understanding of digital twins. We also derive a set of recommendations for managers and outline opportunities for future research.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2713586.a: Prior research has documented that ESG performance is associated with lower operational risk at the firm level, yet whether it also reduces the supply chain risk that the focal firm faces in its trading relationships remains underexplored. Grounded in resource dependence theory, this study examines how a focal firm’s ESG performance affects its supply chain risk, using a sample of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2009 to 2025. The results indicate that ESG performance significantly reduces the supply chain risk faced by the focal firm. Mediation analysis shows that this effect is partly transmitted through reductions in partner composition concentration and geographic concentration. At the network level, the focal firm’s ESG performance is negatively associated with the supply chain risk of its direct partners, secondary partners, and same-tier peers.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2714618.a: Article title: Innovative approaches in reshaping the supply chain for societal challengesAuthors: Fornasiero, R., and Zangiacomi, A.Journal: Production Planning & ControlDOI: https://doi.org/10.10...

10.1080/09537287.2026.2717305.a: The Fifth Hand is an emerging behavioural–institutional theory of project behaviour that explains infrastructure project cost mis-performance through interactions among individual decisions, organisational dynamics, and institutional logics. However, the ecological rationality underpinning these interactions has remained implicit, limiting understanding of why cost mis-performance in infrastructure projects arises in volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous conditions. Our paper addresses this gap by integrating Gigerenzer’s cognitive (mind ↔ environment) and Smith’s institutional (institution ↔ environment) traditions of ecological rationality to develop what we term nested rationality. This integration establishes the ecological foundations of the Fifth Hand, explaining how organisational and institutional environments influence reasoning strategies and the interpretation and treatment of recognised cost pressures under uncertainty. Our paper extends the Fifth Hand by providing an ecological explanation of infrastructure cost mis-performance and identifying principles for improving decision-making throughout an infrastructure project’s pre-and-post contract phases.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2718425.a: Manufacturing companies face a persistent challenge: maintaining quality stability amidst fluctuating process conditions and material variability. While traditional quality management emphasises technical standardisation, this paper argues that quality is actively stabilised through distributed routines and human sensemaking on the shop floor. Using an inductive, multiple-case study of four manufacturing firms and 32 interviews, we employ the Gioia methodology to identify seven core dimensions of quality stabilisation: Process-Input Fit, Ripple Effects of Small Process Changes, Real-Time Quality Sensemaking, Tacit-to-Standard Translation, Precision Drift Anticipation, the Reliability-Intervention Loop, and Machine–Human Synchronisation Routines. We develop a diagnostic framework that identifies recurring patterns associated with possible gaps in formal process control. The seven dimensions do not constitute a new control system. Nor do the interview data demonstrate that local interventions improved performance. The framework indicates when managers should examine an existing SOP or Process Quality Control Plan for unvalidated adjustments or possible statistical tampering risks.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2719623.a: How cross-border e-commerce platforms facilitate firms in responding to disruptions is growing to become important to improve supply chain responsiveness. Existing literature focuses on isolated disruptions and the adoption of static adoption of technologies; this research investigates the responsiveness affordances enabled by cross-border e-commerce platforms applied in facilitating small and medium-sized enterprises’ (SMEs) efforts to respond to compounding disruptions. This research follows a process approach, combining a retrospective and real-time perspective to report on qualitative inquiries with experienced informants from 15 SMEs in the manufacturing industry. The results offer a process model revealing how cross-border e-commerce platforms enabled affordances for SMEs’ responsiveness strategies to evolve throughout the Trade War and COVID-19, and also unpack the underlying logic behind the dynamic.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2730017.a: Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies have significant potential to improve supply chain performance, yet organisations often struggle to realise these benefits in practice. Drawing on Structural Ambidexterity Theory, this study examines how specific I4.0 technologies affect core supply chain functions, identifies the principal barriers to implementation, and explores how organisational and sectoral characteristics influence implementation success. The study conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with supply chain directors, digital transformation leaders, and I4.0 consultants across the automotive, pharmaceutical, food and beverage, construction, and high-technology manufacturing sectors. Data were analysed using a three-stage thematic coding process (open, axial, and selective coding) anchored in Simsek et al. (Citation2009) partitional ambidexterity framework. The findings reveal that different I4.0 technologies generate distinct impacts across supply chain functions. Base technologies, including IoT, sensors, machine learning-driven forecasting, robotics, and big data analytics, deliver measurable improvements in demand planning, inventory management, manufacturing operations, and logistics through enhanced visibility, automation, and operational efficiency. In contrast, advanced technologies such as AI-driven decision intelligence, digital twins, simulation, and augmented reality offer greater transformative potential but require substantially higher levels of organisational learning, experimentation, and integration capability. The study further identifies five interconnected implementation barriers: process immaturity, legacy system integration challenges, human resistance to change, workforce capability gaps, and investment uncertainty. Organisational culture, leadership commitment, firm size, and sector-specific regulatory and competitive conditions are found to shape the success and pace of I4.0 adoption. Building on these findings, the study argues that I4.0 adoption creates a fundamental socio-technical tension between exploitation and exploration. Structural separation of exploitative and explorative technology initiatives, enabled through cloud computing and big data analytics, emerges as a viable mechanism for managing this tension. The study extends the partitional ambidexterity framework through the concept of Connected Partitioning and introduces Virtual Integration as a digital mechanism linking differentiated capability streams. It further proposes Structural Buffering as a mechanism for protecting explorative technology initiatives from the socio-technical resistance concentrated in that domain, and identifies a sequential ambidexterity pathway in which exploitative stabilisation is a precondition for explorative capability. The research provides a theoretically grounded and empirically rich understanding of I4.0-enabled supply chain transformation and offers actionable guidance for managers navigating digital transformation initiatives.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2733697.a: Public healthcare providers routinely fail racialised and minoritised populations, producing not only systemic alienation, but also inequitable and unjust service operations outcomes. Framed as a management challenge with mapped interactions in Scotland, we identify a dominant vicious cycle in which insufficient professional cultural competence degrades the service ecosystem, eroding equitable access and creating systemic bottlenecks. Two further reinforcing loops deter service use: Data Fear, driven by surveillance anxiety, and Community Stigma, rooted in reputational harm. Both function as demand-suppression mechanisms, separating need from observed use in ways conventional capacity planning cannot detect. To disrupt these three interlocking cycles, we propose a phased implementation strategy anchored by a community-led Software-as-a-Service reverse-training artefact embedding continuous professional development. Equity and justice should be treated as measurable dimensions of service quality, on a par with reliability and responsiveness, rather than peripheral ethical concerns.

10.1080/09537287.2026.2733698.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has recently gained attention as a technology that supports supply chain decision-making due to its unique natural language capabilities. In this context, it is seen as a top-layer augmentation to traditional analytical and optimisation-based technologies, accelerating decision support needed to keep businesses competitive. While extant literature largely discusses the conceptual potentials of GenAI, empirical evidence on its implications for human-AI collaboration and its boundaries with other AI technologies remains limited. Therefore, the present study adopts an abductive qualitative approach to explore GenAI-based decision-making through semi-structured interviews with experts. The empirical data were analysed using thematic analysis and subsequently interpreted through the lens of a recent AI decision-making framework. By theorising the empirical insights, this study clarifies GenAI’s current role as a cognitive decision-support layer rather than an autonomous decision-maker, along with its limitations. The findings contribute to the literature by providing empirical validation of GenAI as an augmentative technology and by offering evidence-based guidance on how organisations can responsibly leverage GenAI to enhance decision quality, operational efficiency, and operational resilience.

10.1080/095372870412331313357.a: One of the significant effects of the implementation of an open-door policy in China is that many Hong Kong-based manufacturers’ production lines have been moved to China to take advantage of the lower production costs, lower wages and lower rental costs, but as a consequence the finished products must be delivered from China to Hong Kong. It has been discovered that, given a noisy set of data, distribution management cannot determine an appropriate strategy, and hence unnecessarily high expenditure is being incurred. In this paper, a stochastic linear programming model is developed to solve cross-border distribution problems in an environment of uncertainty. Under different economic growth scenarios, decision-makers can determine a long-term distribution strategy, including the optimal delivery routes and the optimal vehicle fleet composition. A set of data from a Hong Kong-based manufacturing company is used to demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our model. The analysis of two possible changes in distribution strategies is also considered. The proposed model can provide appropriate distribution strategy with fleet management in an uncertain environment.

10.1080/09537289008919289.a: This paper attempts to provide a universal conceptual framework for the function of production control. The existing literature on production control deals mainly with the mechanical engineering industry. This paper attempts first to provide a framework suitable for all types of production industry. The second purpose of the paper is to support the view that the function of production planning uses production engineering skills to plan the means to be used to make products, and production control uses the very different scheduling skills to programme the work. There is some confusion in the literature about the division between these functions. Here the term ‘production control’ is preferred to the term ‘production planning and control’. Finally, there is confusion in the literature over the meaning of the terms ‘stock control’ and ‘inventory control’. This paper adopts the convention that stock control is an ‘ordering system based on re-order levels’; inventory control is a feed-back control system for controlling the level of investment in a company, and both are integral parts of the function of production control.

10.1080/09537289008919290.a: Effective control of manufacturing processes depends on accurate, timely recording of data from the shop floor. Data collected as result of this is translated into information which may be the basis for real-time control or later management decisions. Thus there is a need for a data capture and analysis mechanism which operates reliably, quickly and accurately. This mechanism is called the monitoring function. The monitoring function comprises of three distinct elements, namely: data capture; data analysis and decision support. The data capture system collects all the relevant information from the shop floor and then this is ‘massaged’ by the data analysis mechanism to produce real-time and historical reports which aid the decision making process in the manufacturing system. This paper outlines the development of a software tool for the control of the manufacturing operation at the operational level (i.e. quasi real-time) and describes in detail the development and use of software modules to support the monitoring activities within a simulation environment.

10.1080/09537289008919291.a: This paper considers the problem of scheduling and sequencing jobs on machines in a two-stage production process. The problem is motivated by a real-world application concerning a major paper products plant which produces business forms. Here, the printing and the collating operations constitute the two production stages. We develop a model for this problem and propose a solution approach based on the decoupling of the problem into two single stage problems. Each single stage problem, which is the main focus of this paper, is further decomposed into an allocation subproblem and a sequencing subproblem of jobs on machines. Both exact and heuristic algorithms are developed for these subproblems. An overall scheme is proposed for linking together the information and solutions provided by these decomposed system components. Different versions of the algorithm are tested on industrial data, and recommendations are made for implementation.

10.1080/09537289008919292.a: The use of Material Requirement Planning (MRP) for planning and control of cellular (Group Technology based) production systems is an approach to improve batch manufacturing. Specifically a single cycle MRP system called Period Batch Control (PBC) was suggested as an appropriate model for scheduling this type of production system. The production/operations management literature lacks a study of the performance of multi-cycles MRP systems employing the traditional lot-sizing technique in a cellular environment. This paper presents a model of a cellular production system and a heuristic lot-sizing procedure which is based on the trade off between set-up cost and inventory carrying cost for such systems controlled by MRP.

10.1080/09537289008919293.a: Much planning and control in production is ‘action oriented’, that is, action is preferred to the application of insight and understanding. Despite the fact that almost every section and department of an industrial enterprise is involved, production management has become a specialized function closely attached to the computer department. In order to benefit from the potential combined effects (synergy) of modern technology we need to include many aspects and disciplines. This has called for a new, situational approach to production management which accepts the complexity of reality and strives for insight, which focuses attention on the mutual interplay between involved sections, and which considers production management as an integral part of the industrial enterprise. The result of adopting this new approach is presented in this and a subsequent paper. The present paper first discusses how to define the role of production in a corporate context. It includes a comparison of actual performance with the production mission. And a problem matrix is introduced as a method to disclose the actual interplay between individuals and sections in an industrial enterprise. This paper also introduces the notion of a Production Management Concept which is defined as an overall, coherent picture of the way in which the production management role is to be carried out. Three examples of a production management concept are discussed, illustrating three different production modes. It is shown how a concept may stimulate the development of mutual agreements among interested parties and serve as a framework for discussing various planning methods and principles. In a subsequent issue, a second paper will address the planning of implementation of production management systems design, including organizational and behavioural aspects as well as project management theory and practice.

10.1080/09537289008919294.a: The movement to just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing philosophies and techniques will be critical to the survival of many manufacturing entities that compete in the world-wide marketplace. Unfortunately, the process of converting to JIT can be a survival-threatening experience in itself, but this need not be the case. This paper will describe several simple, low-risk, and low-cost approaches used at the Lake Stevens Instrument Division (LSID) of Hewlett-Packard to successfully achieve a work-orderless JIT manufacturing environment. In particular, the paper will describe how to gain most of the benefits of JIT in a low-volume, high-mix environment without incurring the complexities and risks associated with a complete post-deduct (backflush) JIT implementation. Three phases of implementation will be described: a pull process with work-orders, a work-orderless pull process with distinct stores and WIP inventories, and a partial implementation of a post-deduct process with online storage of combined stores and WIP inventory. The paper will also discuss the risks and trade-offs associated with implementing a post deduct process and present the results that can be achieved with a less complex strategy for achieving JIT manufacturing

10.1080/09537289008919295.a: Advances in the technology of manufacturing planning, control and operation have made conventional cost accounting practices not only obsolete but dangerous. As a portion of total factory cost, direct labour costs have declined dramatically due to improved quality materials, fewer interruptions, automation and robotics. Overhead costs, conversely, have increased greatly and the fixed components now predominate. Charts of accounts contain many trivial items and lack those now considered very important. This article presents the needed revisions.

10.1080/09537289008919299.a: In the future, the competitive strength of industry will depend on its ability to realize flexible production systems, to install intelligent EDP-systems and to link them to a goal-orientated logistic system. Currently, a lot of new strategies, concepts and approaches for production arc being promoted and discussed, often in a spirit of controversy: CIM (computer integrated manufacturing), 'production logistics’, and JIT (just-in-time production) have become familiar concepts which have one thing in common: new structures in production will be necessary. However, the overall effect of CIM is often very small in comparison to the investment for realizing this concept. The main reason is that such projects are missing a logistic orientation. A continuous flow of information and material as envisaged by the logistics principle requires not only that all automation components can be integrated on the technical level, but also that all relevant functions and sectors can be integrated organizationally.

10.1080/09537289008919300.a: Finding the utilization of a set of machines in a shop floor of a production system by the ratio delay method is a well-known practice in conventional time and motion studies. In this method, the desired reliability of the study is preset and subsequently the data are collected to achieve that reliability. I do not continuously review the reliability in this method while conducting the study nor do I measure the benefit-cost ratio of the undergoing study. In this paper, I describe a method to determine the utilization of a set of production facilities and continuously review the reliability achieved at the end of each survey period. The random observations about the machine status generate a utilization profile of a set of machines on a continuous time scale. Based on the benefit-cost ratio, this method provides us with an information as to when the study has to be stopped in a real time situation. The study is substantiated with a case study and an indication of further research.

10.1080/09537289008919301.a: This paper provides an appreciation of the effects of technology on the manufacturing process. Essentially, it is argued that technology is increasingly becoming an essential and endogenous part of the manufacturing process. Internal and dynamical processes related to the introduction and the absorption of technology are also leading manufacturing systems to be more complex, hierarchical, integrated and far more sensitive to external disturbances. It is also argued that technology induces its own growth process, triggering a process of perpetual technological challenge and change.The paper explains both how and why technology is inducing such changes and how it can be dealt with.

10.1080/09537289008919302.a: The paper deals with different viewpoints in product structuring knowledge. Special interest is paid to a new viewpoint called control structure. The necessity for such a concept is based on the penetration of product oriented manufacturing systems (factories, workshops and cells) together with the related distribution of production management decision making. Control structure is an aggregated control oriented viewpoint on the product structure hiding the details of the work operations and materials requirements at the lower levels of decision making. Thus control structures are also intended for the integration and loosely coupled co-ordination of control units. The paper also strongly advocates the application of interactive graphics in the manipulation of product structure information. A practical system developed is demonstrated as a vehicle for implementing the concepts introduced.

10.1080/09537289008919303.a: Several examples of unsuccessful planning and implementation of a new production management system point to a need for a more careful initial planning of where to go. Furthermore, there is a need for defining the scope of an improvement project at an early stage. A new approach to production management proposes as a task for all sections of an industrial enterprise. This paper aims to provide a structured approach to planning and managing a production management improvement process. By offering a framework and a number of methods we provide means for structuring a creative problem solving process. Three points of views are combined: (i) a methodology for dealing with the technical matters of production management, (ii) a project management approach to structuring and planning the improvement process, and (iii) a behavioural approach in which organizational learning processes play an essential role. The paper follows a previous paper in this journal (Riis 1990) in which a new approach to production management was outlined, and a technical stream of activities was presented, e.g. analysis and diagnosis, development of a production management concept, design of a production management system, and design for an information system

10.1080/09537289008919304.a: Over the past two decades, there have been critical developments in both manufacturing planning analysis and computer based decision tools, but there has been very little integration of the two. Planning approaches of the 70s and early 80s were simplified partly because it was so difficult to map out and organize the complexity of strategy concepts in any manageable way. Within this paper the use of computer based decision support systems is advocated to help achieve an effective business strategy by understanding the key business dimensions and the fundamental connections between them. The implicaiions of strategy support systems are addressed in the context of their ability to provide managers with a richer model of the business environment. This model should incorporate decision making constraints and qualitative factors heretofore neglected in management decision making processes. Specifically the paper discusses issues concerning master planning activity in a manufacturing business. The paper highlights some of the shortcomings of traditional master planning mechanisms and sheds some light on potential computer based support systems which will provide for higher levels of understanding and facilitate improvements in the quality of management decision making. The use of AI techniques (semantic nets, frames and rule-based paradigms, etc.) as well as conventional decision support processes are proposed in the contcxtof their suitability in representing the problem of master planning.

10.1080/09537289008919310.a: Complexity is a serious problem with respect to the application of information technology in the field of production management. This paper presents an overview of the more fundamental problems encountered and proposes a solution for some of those problems in the form of modular decomposition of the conceptual database structure. It is argued that the complexity of information systems is closely connected to the complexity of the organization. Therefore a condition for the realization of integrated information systems for production management is a simplification of the organizational structure by way of defunctionalization and the forming of autonomous units.

10.1080/09537289008919311.a: Two approaches for constructing control charts for quality assurance when the observations are in the form of linguistic data are presented. Both approaches are based on fuzzy set theory and use fuzzy subsets to model the linguistic terms used to describe product quality. They differ in the interpretation of the control limits and in the procedure used to reduce the fuzzy subsets to scalars for determining the chart parameters. The results obtained with simulated data suggest that, on the basis of sensitivity to process shifts, the control charts for linguistic data perform better than conventional p control charts. The number of linguistic terms used in classifying the observations was found to influence the sensitivity of these control charts. The transformation method used to obtain the representative values and the amount of fuzziness do not seem to affect the performance of either type of control charts.

10.1080/09537289008919312.a: This paper discusses the implementation of a knowledge-based system for the dynamic scheduling of a two-stage production process. It is an interactive, real-time, menu-driven system written in Prolog. The system architecture is delineated and the rules and problem-solving logic to be used under various dynamic situations are described. Results of a sample system test session are included to illustrate its use.

10.1080/09537289008919313.a: This paper presents the results of an empirical investigation of one of the most common yet least optimized production management practices—expediting. The intention of this study was to generate quantitative insight into issues that underlie expediting decision making, such as the relative frequency of various causes of expediting, commonly used expediting strategies and tactics, and the interaction of expediting and the production scheduling environment in use. The study centered around a survey sent to 1768 manufacturing staff personnel, with 182 usable questionnaires returned. It is hoped that the data and conclusions presented in this paper will be of use to production management researchers who are interested in expediting as a managerial decision.

10.1080/09537289008919314.a: While simulation has been used in manufacturing for many years, predominantly for facility design, it is within the last few years, that simulation languages have been developed to a point where they can be used on a day-to-day basis to generate schedules and predict their performance. This paper describes our use of different modelling techniques to develop a production schedule generation system. An example describing a system for a small- to medium-sized order producing company using SIMAN/CINEMA is included. While addressing the shortcomings of existing scheduling systems it is shown how the approach taken is a feasible way of creating a dynamic goal-driven simulation-based production scheduler. The paper does not aim to describe an ‘off the shelf’ scheduling system product, but rather to give an overview to methods, techniques and experiences which enable us rapidly to tailor a simulation-based scheduling system to the specific needs of a company.

10.1080/09537289008919318.a: . It has been empirically observed that productivity improves as production continues due to system 'learning’, but that it deteriorates once the activity is stopped due to system 'forgetting’. Both learning and forgetting follow an exponential form with a 'doubling factor’ ranging between 0.75 and 0.98. We review and critique two previously proposed models, correct some minor errors in them, and expand one of them to accommodate a finite horizon. We also propose a new model that is more in harmony with the established learning function, for the determination of the optimal number and size of the lots in the finite and infinite horizon. The methodology used throughout is dynamic programming. We investigate the impact of all three models on the optimal lot sires and their costs, and establish the functional relations between the total cost and the various factors affecting them.

10.1080/09537289008919319.a: . In international co-operative knockdown production systems (ICKDPS), much longer transportation lead-time than production lead-time to procure component parts is required, because the parts are generally containerized by ship. In this paper, in order to determine an economical buffer stock level for a more reliable ICKDPS, a pull-type ordering system which considers the backorder for compensating for shortage of component parts is developed for the ICKDPS as a three-stage production, inventory and transportation system with the concept of 'just-in-time’ production systems. In addition, the effects of transportation lead-time and buffer stock level on the quantity of backlogs and the probability of requirement are clarified by simulation.

10.1080/09537289008919320.a: . An empirical study explores the business environment, the nature of manufacturing, and the planning cycle, using a sample of enterprises with seasonally-biased sales profiles for their products. This enables both the principles and the practicalities of aggregate planning to stand comparison with the observed rubric of manufacturing management. The conclusion is that neither is germane to industry, and that, in general, practitioners develop an effective (broad) manufacturing strategy with an appropriate resources-acquisition programme. The master production schedule then strikes an acceptable balance between productivity, flexibility, and financial risk.

10.1080/09537289008919321.a: . The small to medium-sized job-shop manufacturing industry can benefit most from the implementation of computer integrated manufacturing (CIM) technology, to meet the increasing demand for high-quality and economically priced products. The injection mould making industry is a typical representative for this group, where a manufacturer would generally produce moulds which consist of parts that are standard to every mould type or very similar. Thus, manufacturing techniques, such as group technology (GT), and production planning and control (information) management systems could make significant contributions in improving the efficiency of design and production operations. The objective of the project, presented in this paper, was the development of a GT-based classification and coding (C/C) system for injection mould parts especially for the design and process planning phases, and the development of a production planning and shop-floor control (SFC) information management system. An extensive investigation was carried out on existing GT-based C/C systems. This investigation, followed by a thorough examination of many injection mould parts for determining geometric similarities, led to the development of part families (classes) required for GT implementation. An OPITZ-type GT system was developed, thereafter, for the C/C of the manufactured parts of the target company. The production planning and control software that has been developed for the target company utilizes a relational data base management system. It consists of 13 application programs, which provide a tool of organizing information for efficient production planning and SFC. The programs are designed to cover all manufacturing operations of a job from the proposal to the final testing stage. Shop orders and dispatch lists are created using this software for effective and prioritized SFC. Shop status and job status reports are generated based on feedback information received through time card entries.

10.1080/09537289008919322.a: . A hierarchical production planning model is developed for a forming facility of a major fibreglass manufacturer. The model establishes aggregate quarterly quantities for families of products, monthly disaggregate production quantities for end-items within these families, and a weekly sequencing schedule of end-items. A key feature of the planning system is its ability to decompose total set-up cost into primary and secondary components and to account appropriately for each component at a distinct level of the planning hierarchy. The mathematical programming formulations, the accompanying solution algorithms, and the results of their application to nine months of actual company demand and cost data are presented.

10.1080/095372890500088001.a: An important variable affecting the production throughput in the wafer fabrication photolithography area is the work-in-process (WIP) level of control wafers. Previous research work has focused on control wafers downgrading problem, and little work has been done for WIP level of control wafers. The objective of this paper is to develop methods for estimating the WIP level of control wafers for each grade, while maintaining the same level of production throughput. Two factors are considered, the re-entrant of control wafers within the same grade and the downgrading of control wafers among different grades. Under pulling control production environment, a multi-loop algorithm is developed for estimating the WIP control wafers for each grade. We conduct some simulation experiments based on a real-world factory production environment to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. The results show that the algorithm is an efficient tool for estimating the cycle time and WIP level for each grade of control wafers.

10.1080/09537289108919325.a: This study, which has been undertaken since 1986, followed several leading japanese and American manufacturers by time-series. In the course of the research activities we found that some of the manufacturers were undergoing a ‘paradigm shift’ in their way of thinking of manufacturing. We labelled the old manufacturing philosophy ‘Business-as-usual’ and the new thinking as ‘Holonic manufacturing’. The value system in which the manufacturing network must live has to be agreeable with Holonic manufacturing. Mass (economy-of-scale) production has a value system different to that of‘new wave’. Enough work has been carried out to make holonic manufacturing a bright vision. For the leading manufacturers, however, truly attaining it is a route filled with many obstacles—they have to create the changes to force the paradigm shift.

10.1080/09537289108919326.a: The planning and control of manufacturing systems is a complex activity involving a myriad of interrelated decisions and optimization algorithms. In a computer integrated manufacturing system (CIMS) these decisions and algorithms span several functions, require information from several sources, and have consequences in several sectors of CIMS. Building decision systems for such a complex environment requires an effective plan. This plan must identify information flows, decision modules, and relevant interrelationships. This paper presents an approach for the development of such a plan, for the production planning and control component of CIMS. The plan is based primarily on the integrated computer aided manufacturing (ICAM) definition models, and is developed using structured analysis.

10.1080/09537289108919327.a: Research into the effect of three factors on four major system performance measures for pull system design and control are reviewed. The three factors are: (1) qualitative or quantitative nature of the approach, (2) traditional production control or pull system approach, and (3) systems/integrative characteristics of the approach for the performance measures. The four performance measures are: (I) throughput, (2) quality, (3) material Dow, and (4) flexibility. Articles were evaluated in terms of the performance measures and factors with several articles discussed in depth, Journals and other sources were chosen to be searched based on the source having published refereed articles related to pull system performance evaluation. Articles on quantitative pull systems are not well represented in the literature. Traditional approach methods

10.1080/09537289108919328.a: The service times at a work station in a production system can be defined by one or more probability distributions. This paper reports the effect of different service time distributions on the performance of a pull system. Simulation has been used as a tool to investigate the performance of such a system. The measures of performance used in the study are the average machine utilization, waiting times of kanban and work-in-process, and output rate at different coefficients of variation of the service times. Conclusions are made and an indication of further research is given.

10.1080/09537289108919329.a: Automated guided-vehicle (AGV) systems are gaining increasing acceptance in modern manufacturing facilities primarily because of the versatility they offer. As the flexibility and complexity of these systems increase, the requirements of the design effort and the routeing and scheduling system grow. In this paper we provide a review of the literature relevant to the system design, routeing and scheduling, and justification and implementation of AGV systems.

10.1080/09537289108919330.a: It is not an uncommon problem that a finished product cannot be delivered to its customer due to order change. In many real-life applications, such as rack-mounted computer products, it is possible to reconfigure a product by altering the combination of its components. Therefore, an inventory item, resulting from a cancelled order, can be handled in one of two ways: (1) keep the product in storage for a future order; or (2) send the product back to the manufacturing Door for reconfiguration in accordance with a new order A wise decision can be made by evaluating the trade-off between the inventory cost and the conversion cost. This paper presents an optimization procedure for achieving the minimum-cost solution. The problem is formulated by a quadratic programming model. Under a fairly general condition, the problem can be converted into a standard capacitated transportation problem and, therefore, can be solved efficiently. The cost structure, problem formulation, and solution technique arc discussed.

10.1080/09537289108919331.a: Production flow analysis (PFA) was used to plan the groups and families for group technology (GT) in a factory making hoists. First, factory flow analysis (FFA) was used to make a division into departments, which completed all the pans they made. Group analysis (GA) was then used to divide these departments into groups, which again completed all the parts they made. The results of the study supports the hypothesis that outside the process industries and some types of mass production, where continuous line flow is preferable, it is always possible to achieve a total division into groups, with few, if any, exceptions.

10.1080/09537289108919332.a: This paper focuses on the attempt to implement Japanese manufacturing technology, viz. zero inventories (ZI) and just-in-time production (JIT) in Chinese manufacturing industries with the objective of raising productivity. In order to study the implications of JIT in Chinese manufacturing industries, a method of analysis is presented for the implementation of ZI and JIT with a view to identifying their suitability and reliability in that environment. In addition, suggestions are given for the successful implementation of ZI and JIT in China.

10.1080/09537289108919333.a: An investigation of non-routine operations at one of the busiest airports in Louisiana and the application of basic forecasting methodology to the same during a 3-year period, which included a turning point in the non-routine operations, is reported. It is established that complex, dynamic, independent demand forecasting does not necessarily require advanced forecasting models.

10.1080/09537289108919335.a: This paper describes a process planning system for sheet metal parts. This system has capabilities to deliver process planning data just in time. The change of tools, processes and even machines for manufacturing of the parts is possible at the shop door after design has been finished. The sequence of the production planning steps carried out can be changed. In this way the system can be adapted to the requirements of different sheet metal manufacturing companies. More detailed information is given about the methods used for nesting of the workpieces on the sheets to be produced.

10.1080/09537289108919336.a: A procedure has been developed for finding optimal solutions to the problem of minimizing tardiness scheduling for a wide variety of constraints. As most practical problems are much larger than could be solved economically by this procedure, the idea of using the lower bound as a decision rule for developing a single, near-optimal solution was developed. The experiments on these decision rules showed that they might profitably be used in place of other rules for certain applications.

10.1080/09537289108919337.a: Petri nets and their supersets have been used since the 1950s as a basis for systems analysis and simulation. This paper describes a methodology for performing static analyses of complex, dynamic systems based on an extension of timed Petri nets, activity cycle diagrams (ACDs). ACDs are introduced and the method for transforming them into a static analysis table is given (examples arc also provided). Limitations of the method are described, and the use of static analysis is discussed in the areas of system design, capacity planning and control. An implementation of the method in C provides interactive capabilities.

10.1080/09537289108919338.a: An alternative strategy is proposed for setting safety stocks to achieve a fixed service level. The approach involves scheduling order releases earlier in the inventory cycle instead of carrying a fixed safety stock based directly on a stockout probability. It is shown that, when combined with a fixed reorder quantity, the alternative strategy results in lower expected carrying costs for a stationary probability distribution of lead time demand.

10.1080/09537289108919339.a: A flexible manufacturing system (FMS), is a complex association of computer-controlled equipment, automated material handling systems, computer control software, and people. The development of such an association can be elaborate, requiring experts from a number of functional disciplines which, when brought together, must operate as a fully integrated, design group. This group, if it is to cope with the many operational as well as organizational difficulties that arise, must be supported by tools and methodologies that can reduce the effects of these difficulties and make the whole design process more effective. This paper deals with the development and operation of FMS from the perspective of an FMS user who is involved in designing and implementing such a complex system. The paper looks first at development issues around the implementation of complex projects such as an FMS. It examines the structure of the project team, tools to be used in preparing specifications, and finally the stages for project implementation and control. It then looks at the operation of a typical FMS. It examines the input, output, and functions of a FMS and takes a view of the internal architecture of the FMS controller.

10.1080/09537289108919340.a: A non-linear 0–1 integer programming formulation of the problem of grouping parts and machines in the presence of alternate process plans in Flexible Manufacturing Systems is presented. An iterative solution procedure based on the decomposition of the original non-linear model into two linear 0–1 integer programming models is suggested to solve the formulation. Application of the formulation and the solution procedure are illustrated using an example.

10.1080/09537289108919341.a: An attempt is made in the paper to study the available literature about flexible manufacturing systems and structure them into a synoptic framework. The purpose of the study is to capture the varied perspectives of the industries and researchers and to provide some conceptual directions for integrating them into the planning, design and implementation of such systems.

10.1080/09537289108919342.a: All over the world the number of FMSs is actually increasing. This paper describes the principal structure of such FMSs, and a method to model their functionality and topology in a hierarchical way. Steps of system introduction are designated. The need for higher qualification of operators—induced by their increasing responsibility—is shown.

10.1080/09537289108919343.a: It is more than 40 years since the idea of Group Technology (GT) was developed, and even longer since Production Control systems—which today arc called Just-In-Time (JIT) systems—were first used in manufacturing. These two approaches, which give simple material flow, with very low stocks, have provided the foundation for Japan's present day superiority in manufacturing. They have, however, been very slow to gain acceptance in the West. This paper studies the reasons for this slow progress in the West. It sees these changes as essential for our survival, and makes some suggestions for improving the rate of progress.

10.1080/09537289108919344.a: We present some thoughts on the practice of just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing. The discussion is focused on three building blocks of JIT manufacturing, namely, waste elimination, workplace organization and total employee involvement. Important implementation issues for a successful JIT program are also considered.

10.1080/09537289108919347.a: It is becoming increasingly important for manufacturing organizations to articulate clear and coherent manufacturing strategies that support their long term business objectives. In particular, manufacturing strategy should take conscious account of the competitive posture adopted by the organization in each of the product/market segments in which it has decided to participate. This paper discusses the various ways in which a systemic manufacturing strategy can contribute to an organization's competitiveness, and the processes by which such a strategy can be developed. Some important and often neglected issues concerning the development of the individual components of a manufacturing strategy are examined and the problems and issues of strategy implementation are discussed.

10.1080/09537289108919348.a: A Double Shuttle Automated Storage/Retrieval operating on a Four Command Cycle is studied in this paper. A retrieval sequencing heuristic along with an approximation for the expected command cycle time is presented in the system. A lower bound is also developed for the mean four command cycle times for various retrieval block sizes and a number of open locations. The throughput of a double shuttle automated storage/retrievalsystem(AS/RS)working on the four command cycles under the heuristic is compared with the that of a single

10.1080/09537289108919349.a: Problems associated with perishable or outdating products arise in many areas of inventory and production man agement. Many commodities exist whose value does not remain constant over time during transportation, holding stock, etc. Significant work has been done to describe optimal ordering policies for items which have a fixed lifetime. In this paper, per ishable inventory models subject to stochastic procurement leadtinie both on LIFO (Last In First Out) and FIFO (First In First Out) issuing policies are considered with cither zero or 1 unit leadtinie. First, assumptions and notation used throughout the paper are given. FIFO and LIFO models are then con structed, and the existence of the optimal ordering policies and theirpropertiesare clarified. Finally, significantresults are illustrated for the relationship among inventory on hand, delay probability of procurement and optimal ordering policies.

10.1080/09537289108919350.a: We consider three well-known production-inventory control systems: Material Requirements Planning, Just-In-Time and Bottleneck Scheduling. Each system was developed with a specific production environment in mind, and it would therefore be naive to assume that these systems apply to any situation. Most factories would benefit from a hybrid system which carefully weighs functionalities from different systems to fit the problem at hand.
